summary: Western Lake Erie light on a stone pier off Colchester, Ontario, lit 3 November 1885 after a lightship and a failed caisson; boat access only, closed to visitors.

structures.type: hexagonal wooden tower on a circular stone pier

structures.note: LighthouseFriends describes it as red with a white oval daymark; the Lighthouse Directory as painted red with a slatted daymark; the Coast Guard list as a white skeleton tower.

access.note: Site and tower closed; reachable only by boat (Lighthouse Directory).

visit.note: Lighthouse Directory: accessible only by boat; site and tower closed.

events.note: Hackett brothers of Amherstburg lay a keel for a new lightship to replace a vessel on the reef.
Parliament agrees to pay an annual subsidy of $500 towards the lightship; raised to $700 by 1876.
Parliament appropriates $5,000 towards a lighthouse on a pier on the reef; tenders received from $15,500 to $37,555.
Lightship driven from station, cut in two by ice floes and sunk; crew rescued by a passing steamer. Year approximate: LighthouseFriends places it after a late-1880 request to withdraw her.
Iron caisson for the foundation destroyed in August. Mower County Transcript attributes it to a severe storm; Watertown Republican, quoting George J. Wilson, to the cofferdam giving way.
Lightship foundered in a gale on the night of 12 November 1883; Captain James S. Forrest drowned.
Lightship withdrawn once the light was lit.
Fog bell added, tolled every 15 seconds from a belfry on the south side of the tower.
Twelve crib-work piers placed around the stone foundation in the 1890 and 1891 seasons ($9,560.42).
Steel and concrete protection replaces the crib-work; steel bell tower replaces the wooden one; day labour under Fred Forster, $4,955.24.
55 mm diamond vapour installation replaces the duplex lamp.
Fred Malott transfers from Pelee Passage to succeed John Manson, who retires at seventy for failing eyesight.
John B. Knapp begins long service at the lighthouse.
Keeper Knapp and assistant S. Bock stranded at the lighthouse in December when ice blocked boat and walking access.
Station automated; bell discontinued; characteristic changed from fixed white to flashing white.
Skeleton tower replaces the historic wooden lighthouse.

keepers.name: Christopher Robson
keepers.note: First keeper; replaced after roughly six months.

keepers.name: John Manson
keepers.note: Born in Scotland; a former mate of the lightship Dunscomb at Bar Point; retired at seventy for failing eyesight. Listed against 'Colchester Reef, Light and Fog Bell' in the 1906 Department statement (scan 173, printed p. 164) with an appointment date of May 1, 1880 (850 00): checked on the page image. That date conflicts with LighthouseFriends' 1885-1886 start. Written 'Captain Alanson' once in LighthouseFriends, which is evidently Manson.

keepers.name: Fred Malott
keepers.note: Transferred from Pelee Passage Lighthouse. Not confirmed in the Department statements we read.

keepers.name: John B. Knapp
keepers.note: LighthouseFriends roster 'John B. Knapp'; text 'John Knapp'. Station automated in 1936.

keepers.name: S. Bock
keepers.note: Assistant to Knapp; stranded with him in December 1933. Only the December 1933 stay is dated.

keepers.name: James S. Forrest
keepers.note: Sixty-three years old; in charge of George Campbell of Windsor's lightship when she foundered in a gale in November 1883. LighthouseFriends says he and another man drowned; the Rock Island Argus wire report says he was the only man aboard.

wrecks.outcome: Driven from station, cut in two by ice floes and sunk; crew rescued by a passing steamer. Year approximate.
Foundered in a gale; Captain James S. Forrest drowned. LighthouseFriends says another man drowned too; the 13 November 1883 wire report says Forrest alone was on board.

corrections.why: The standing tower is the 1954 skeleton tower; the 1885 structure was the wooden lighthouse, replaced in 1954.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikipedia's infobox (not cited) names Colonel William P. Anderson as builder. LighthouseFriends, quoting the Department, names John E. Askwith as the contractor who completed the light after George Wilson gave up. Askwith is the sourced name; Anderson is unsupported in the sources we read.

The 1906 statement (page image checked) gives May 1, 1880 as Manson's appointment at Colchester Reef. LighthouseFriends dates his charge of the light from the Dunscomb's move in 1885 and its roster gives 1886. The sources do not reconcile these; left open in the story.

notes_for_editor:
Sources. The 1869, 1871, 1876, 1880 to 1885 and 1886 to 1911 facts (lightship subsidies, tenders, Askwith's contract, the 1885 light, the Manson years and the keepers before 1911) come from LighthouseFriends, which quotes the Department's reports. Those reports are not in the local corpus before 1900 and the 1900 to 1924 volumes were searched only for the Colchester entries cited here. The 1885 Department description is the one short quotation kept from LighthouseFriends; the rest are paraphrased.

Newspapers. Three 1883 items cover the caisson and the lightship loss, and one April 1880 item covers the lightship's repair. The Mower County Transcript and the Watertown Republican disagree on the cause of the caisson's loss (storm or cofferdam); LighthouseFriends says storm. The Watertown item reports George J. Wilson's claimed loss of about $10,000 and then describes the cofferdam mishap; it does not say Wilson gave that account, so the story attributes the description to the paper. The Rock Island Argus says Forrest alone was aboard; LighthouseFriends says he and another man drowned. Neither disagreement is settled. Chronicling America searches for 'Askwith' with 'Colchester' found no hits; the contractor's name rests on LighthouseFriends. Two 1881 Chicago Tribune items were seen in search results but their OCR was too damaged to quote.

OCR table rows, checked on the scan images on 2026-10-28: (a) 1906 statement, scan 173 (printed p. 164): 'Manson, John | Colchester Reef, Light and Fog Bell | May 1, 1880 | 850 00': confirmed. The 1880 date conflicts with LighthouseFriends' chronology (see resolved_conflicts) and is stated in the story. (b) The 1911-12 works table (scan 69) has a Colchester reef entry for concrete-protection repairs beside three other stations; the column matching is unclear, so that entry is left out. (c) The 1905 and 1907 Department report lines (scan 44 and scan 48) were read as text; the 1905 line gives Forster's direction and cost but not a labour method, so the story says no more about the method.

Colour of the tower. LighthouseFriends describes the 1954 tower as red with a white oval daymark; the Lighthouse Directory says the whole structure is painted red; the Coast Guard list calls it a white skeleton tower. The story states all three without choosing. Check a recent photograph before the page is published.

Range. The record gives 5.2 nautical miles, which is not in the Coast Guard entry we read (the entry has no range) and is not in any source we read. The 1885 description gave 14 miles, all round. The editor should check the record's range before publication.

Record correction proposed: the standing tower's built year should be 1954, not 1885; the 1885 tower was the wooden lighthouse, replaced in 1954.

Keeper roster: Fred Malott and John B. Knapp are from LighthouseFriends only; no primary Department statement for their service was read. The statement for 1911 onwards was not searched for them.

People. None of the keepers served after 1936, and none is living-person sensitive. The Lake Carriers' Association anecdotes concern Manson's own boat and family in 1911 and earlier; the story keeps them short and names only Manson and his wife as 'his wife'.

Not done: no photos were added (the record's Wikimedia photo was not checked for licence).
